Maria signed in at 12.55 last night, five minutes before curfew, with three friends, all laughing, smelling of chai and roasted corn. She had told her study group she'd join their revision at nine. I asked what she'd do about the revision. She said she'd ask the group for their notes and host a session in her room tomorrow. I've booked the small reading room for them instead. I'll check with her after the test.
– Dilnaz

Tuesday, 2 a.m.
I was supposed to be at Pema's room at nine for the anatomy revision. Instead I went up to the hostel roof with four others because someone said the meteor shower was tonight. We lay on bedsheets and counted streaks. I saw eleven! We shared a flask of cocoa and sang badly and I laughed until my stomach hurt. It was perfect. Honestly perfect. But every time I looked at my phone there was a message from Pema: "coming?" and later just "ok." That "ok" is sitting in my chest now. I'll bring Pema breakfast and my flashcards tomorrow. I don't regret the stars. I just wish they'd come on a Friday.
– Ira

The circus had been in Dharwad for three weeks, and tonight was its last show. Ankita, twenty, lay on her hostel bed with her agronomy notes, listening to the music drifting from the field beyond the college wall.
Jyoti knocked. "We're still studying at nine, right? Soil chemistry, chapter six."
Ankita looked at the notes. Then at her roommates pulling on shoes. "Jyoti... it's the last night."
She went. The trapeze girls flew under the lights, the clowns threw water at the front row, and Ankita screamed with laughter, eating hot peanuts from a paper cone. On the walk back under the streetlights, singing badly, she felt more alive than she had all term.
Then she saw Jyoti's message: "Did chapter six alone. It's long." Ankita's stomach gave a small twist. She typed, "Sorry. Tomorrow I'll bring tea and do it with you, promise." Then she lay back, still smiling.

qa.q: What did Ankita eat at the circus?
qa.a: Hot peanuts from a paper cone.

qa.q: What mix of feelings did Ankita have on the walk back?
qa.a: She felt more alive than she had all term, and then a small twist of guilt when she saw Jyoti's message.

qa.q: What choice did Ankita make after seeing Jyoti's message, and why does it help?
qa.a: She apologised and promised to bring tea and study the chapter tomorrow, which lets her keep the joy of the night while making up for the missed session.

qa.a: Jyoti might feel a little let down and tired from studying alone, though the promise of tea and company may soften it.

In the student hall in Edinburgh, Rosa had promised Tariq they'd go through the statistics past papers at eight. At seven-thirty her flatmates knocked. "Ceilidh at the union, last one before exams! Come on!"
Rosa, twenty, looked at the papers, then at their bright faces. She texted Tariq: "Can we do tomorrow? I'm so sorry."
The hall was hot and packed. A fiddler played, and strangers grabbed her hands and spun her through dances she didn't know. She laughed until her ribs hurt and her hair came loose.
At midnight, sitting on the steps outside with cold air on her face, she checked her phone. Tariq had replied: "Ok. I'll start without you." No emoji, nothing.
Rosa felt a small, sharp pang. She didn't regret the night. She also knew Tariq had waited. She set an alarm for six and wrote, "Breakfast and past papers. My treat."

qa.q: What time did Rosa set her alarm for?
qa.a: For six.

qa.q: What was Rosa feeling when she read Tariq's reply?
qa.a: She felt a small, sharp pang of guilt, while still not regretting the joyful night.

qa.q: What did Rosa choose to do about the missed session, and why is it a good choice?
qa.a: She set an early alarm and offered Tariq breakfast and past papers, which respects her commitment without spoiling the night she enjoyed.

qa.q: How might Tariq have felt when Rosa cancelled?
qa.a: Tariq may have felt disappointed and a bit let down, which shows in the short reply with no emoji.

grounding: It shows a young adult who skips a study session for a late-night dance, enjoys it fully and feels a pinch of guilt as enjoyment and responsibility pull apart.
